sla_notes_intro: Divinity is the academic study of God, of the Christian faith and of the way God has related to human beings. It is also called theology and it builds on the Bible as its main source.
sla_notes_details: The word divinity comes from the Latin divinitas, meaning the quality of being God or godlike, while theology comes from the Greek theos (God) and logos (word or study). Divinity examines the nature and character of God, God's revelation to humankind, the history of God's people, the person and work of Jesus Christ, and how believers should live. Its main branches are biblical studies (Old and New Testament), systematic theology (organised teaching on God, humanity, sin and salvation), church history, and practical or moral theology (ethics, pastoral care and worship). The main sources are the Bible, church tradition, reason and human experience, with the Bible as the final authority. The Protestant Bible has 66 books (39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament). The study of Divinity helps learners to understand faith, to develop moral values, to lead communities and to respect people of other beliefs.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who reads Psalm 23 and explains what it teaches about God as a shepherd who guides and protects is doing divinity: the text is the source, and the student interprets it, relates it to Christian doctrine and applies it to life.
sla_notes_daily_life: Divinity shapes conduct in homes, schools and workplaces through values such as honesty, love, forgiveness and service, and it prepares people for roles such as pastors, chaplains, counsellors, teachers and community leaders.
sla_exercise: What is the meaning of the word theology?::It comes from the Greek theos (God) and logos (word or study), so it means the study of God.||Name the four main branches of Divinity.::Biblical studies, systematic theology, church history and practical (moral) theology.||How many books are in the Protestant Bible?::There are 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament.||Give two reasons for studying Divinity.::It develops moral values and understanding of faith, and it prepares people for leadership and service in the community.

sla_notes_intro: The books of Judges, Samuel and Kings record how ancient Israel was governed, first by judges, then by kings. They show good and bad leadership and how God judged the leaders.
sla_notes_details: Governance is the way authority is exercised to direct the affairs of a people. In Judges (about 1200-1050 BC) Israel had no central government; God raised charismatic leaders such as Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon and Samson who delivered the tribes from oppressors. The book repeats a cycle: the people sin, are oppressed, cry to God, a judge delivers them, and then they sin again, ending with the remark that in those days there was no king and everyone did what was right in their own eyes (Judges 21:25). Samuel was the last judge, a prophet and priest; when the people demanded a king he warned them of the burdens of monarchy (1 Samuel 8) and anointed Saul and later David. Under David and Solomon the united kingdom reached its peak, with Jerusalem as capital and the temple built by Solomon. After Solomon the kingdom split in about 931 BC into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Kings were judged by their loyalty to the covenant, and prophets such as Nathan and Elijah held them accountable, for example when David took Bathsheba and Ahab seized Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21). Lessons include accountability, justice for the poor, avoiding abuse of power and dependence on God.
sla_notes_illustrations: The story of Naboth's vineyard shows governance in practice: King Ahab and Queen Jezebel used false witnesses to kill Naboth and take his land, and the prophet Elijah condemned them, showing that even a king is under God's law.
sla_notes_daily_life: The lessons apply to modern leaders in government, schools and churches: leaders must be accountable, respect property and rights, listen to advisers and serve rather than exploit the people.
sla_exercise: Name two judges of Israel.::Deborah and Gideon (also Samson, Ehud or Othniel).||Who was the last judge and the prophet who anointed Saul and David?::Samuel.||What happened to Israel after the death of Solomon?::The kingdom divided into Israel in the north and Judah in the south.||How did prophets contribute to governance in the time of the kings?::They advised kings and held them accountable, for example Nathan rebuked David and Elijah rebuked Ahab.

sla_notes_intro: Elijah and Elisha were prophets of God in Israel in the ninth century BC. Their ministries show courage in standing for truth against powerful people.
sla_notes_details: A prophet (Hebrew nabi) is a person called by God to speak God's message to the people, and prophecy is that message, which may warn, correct, comfort or foretell. Courage is the ability to do what is right even when one is afraid or in danger. Elijah the Tishbite served during the reign of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel who promoted the worship of Baal. He announced a drought (1 Kings 17:1), confronted Ahab as the troubler of Israel and challenged 450 prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, where fire from God consumed his sacrifice (1 Kings 18). He also condemned the murder of Naboth (1 Kings 21). Elisha succeeded Elijah, received a double portion of his spirit (2 Kings 2), healed Naaman the Syrian of leprosy, helped a widow with oil, raised the Shunammite woman's son and fearlessly advised kings, refusing gifts for his services. Both men trusted God rather than human power.
sla_notes_illustrations: On Mount Carmel Elijah stood alone before the king and hundreds of prophets and said, How long will you go limping between two opinions? He prepared the altar, prayed, and the Lord answered by fire, so the people confessed that the Lord is God.
sla_notes_daily_life: Courage is needed today when a student refuses to cheat, an employee reports corruption or a citizen defends the rights of the weak despite threats.
sla_exercise: Which king and queen did Elijah oppose?::King Ahab and Queen Jezebel.||What happened on Mount Carmel?::Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal, and fire from God consumed his sacrifice, proving that the Lord is God.||Name one miracle done by Elisha.::He healed Naaman of leprosy (or raised the Shunammite's son, or increased the widow's oil).||Define courage in the context of the prophets.::It is standing firm for God's truth and justice even when one faces danger and opposition.

sla_name: Making right decisions at the right time: Elijah and Elisha
sla_assessment_criteria: The courage seen in Elijah’s ministry is well discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Bible|Videos on making right decisions at the right time|Biblical charts|Relevant biblical books as commentaries

sla_notes_intro: Good decisions taken at the right time are a mark of wise leadership. Elijah and Elisha show how faith, prayer and prompt action guide decisions.
sla_notes_details: At Carmel Elijah forced the people to decide between the Lord and Baal, saying they must not waver (1 Kings 18:21), and he acted promptly at the time of sacrifice. After Jezebel threatened him he fled to Mount Horeb in fear, but God met him in a still small voice and sent him back with clear tasks: anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha as successors (1 Kings 19). Elisha made a decisive choice when Elijah called him: he burned his plough, slaughtered his oxen, gave food to the people and followed Elijah, leaving no way back (1 Kings 19:19-21). Later he asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, a right request at the right time (2 Kings 2:9). Steps for right decision-making include praying, gathering facts, seeking advice, weighing consequences by God's word, and acting without delay. Delay or wrong decisions bring loss, as when Ahab spared Ben-hadad against God's command (1 Kings 20).
sla_notes_illustrations: Elisha's decision to follow Elijah immediately shows timely choice: by burning his oxen and plough he showed that he had accepted the call fully and could not go back to his old life.
sla_notes_daily_life: Students face decisions about studies, friends, careers and marriage, and leaders face decisions about budgets and public safety; deciding prayerfully, with advice and on time avoids regret.
sla_exercise: What did God tell Elijah to do at Horeb?::To anoint Hazael as king of Syria, Jehu as king of Israel and Elisha as prophet in his place.||How did Elisha show a firm decision to follow Elijah?::He slaughtered his oxen, burned his plough and followed Elijah.||List three steps for making a right decision.::Pray, gather facts and seek advice, weigh consequences by God's word and then act in time.||Why is timing important in decision making?::Delay can cause loss of opportunity or harm, as seen when Ahab wrongly spared Ben-hadad.

sla_notes_intro: Isaiah chapters 1-12 contain messages of judgment and hope to Judah. They introduce the holiness of God, the sin of the people and the promise of a Messiah.
sla_notes_details: Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Judah in the eighth century BC during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Chapter 1 accuses Judah of rebellion, empty sacrifices and injustice, and invites the people to reason with God: though your sins are like scarlet they shall be white as snow. Chapter 5 is the song of the vineyard, showing that God expected justice but found bloodshed. In chapter 6 Isaiah sees God on the throne, hears the seraphim cry holy, holy, holy, confesses his uncleanness, is cleansed with a live coal and answers, Here am I, send me. Chapter 7:14 gives the sign of Immanuel (God with us) to King Ahaz, chapter 9:6 announces a child called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father and Prince of Peace, and chapter 11 promises a shoot from the stem of Jesse on whom the Spirit rests, bringing a kingdom of peace. Chapter 12 is a song of thanksgiving. Main ideas are God's holiness, judgment on sin, the faithful remnant and messianic hope.
sla_notes_illustrations: In Isaiah 6, when the prophet realised he was a man of unclean lips he was purified, then volunteered for God's work; this shows that God cleanses those he calls.
sla_notes_daily_life: The chapters teach that ritual without justice is worthless, a message relevant to believers who worship on Sunday but exploit workers or cheat customers on Monday.
sla_exercise: Who was Isaiah and when did he prophesy?::He was the son of Amoz who prophesied in Judah in the eighth century BC under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.||What did Isaiah see in chapter 6?::He saw God on a high throne with seraphim crying holy, holy, holy.||Which verse gives the sign of Immanuel?::Isaiah 7:14.||Name two titles of the child announced in Isaiah 9:6.::Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father or Prince of Peace (any two).

sla_notes_intro: Isaiah chapters 40-45 speak to the Jews in exile in Babylon. They bring comfort, declare the greatness of God and promise return from exile.
sla_notes_details: These chapters begin with the words comfort, comfort my people (40:1). They declare that the word of God stands for ever (40:8), that God is the incomparable creator who does not grow weary and who renews the strength of those who wait for him (40:28-31). Chapter 41 tells Israel not to fear because God is with them. The first Servant Song (42:1-4) presents the servant of the Lord who brings justice gently. Chapters 43-44 assure Israel of redemption, and God says I have called you by name, you are mine, and when you pass through the waters I will be with you. Chapter 44 mocks idol makers, showing the foolishness of worshipping wood, and 44:28-45:1 names Cyrus of Persia as God's shepherd and anointed who would allow the exiles to return and rebuild Jerusalem. Chapter 45 stresses that there is no other God and calls all the ends of the earth to turn to him. The main ideas are comfort, monotheism, God's sovereignty over history and redemption.
sla_notes_illustrations: The promise in Isaiah 40:31 that those who wait for the Lord will mount up with wings like eagles was given to discouraged exiles, showing that God gives strength to the weary.
sla_notes_daily_life: People facing job loss, sickness or displacement can draw comfort and hope from these chapters, and the mockery of idols warns against trusting money or power instead of God.
sla_exercise: To whom were Isaiah 40-45 addressed?::To the Jewish exiles in Babylon.||Which foreign king did God call his anointed?::Cyrus of Persia.||What does Isaiah 40:31 promise?::Those who wait for the Lord will renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles.||What is the message of Isaiah 44 about idols?::Idols made by human hands are powerless and foolish, and only the Lord is God.

sla_notes_intro: Isaiah calls people to turn from sin to God and to live a life set apart for God. Repentance and holiness are central to the book.
sla_notes_details: Repentance (Hebrew shuv, to turn back; Greek metanoia, change of mind) means recognising sin, confessing it, turning away from it and returning to God with a changed way of life. In Isaiah 1:16-18 the people are told to wash themselves, cease to do evil, learn to do good, seek justice, correct oppression, defend the fatherless and plead for the widow, and God promises forgiveness. In chapter 6 Isaiah's confession is followed by cleansing and commissioning. Isaiah 55:6-7 invites the wicked to forsake their way and return to the Lord who will abundantly pardon, and chapter 58 explains that true fasting is to loose the bonds of injustice, share bread with the hungry and shelter the poor. A holy life means being set apart for God, showing his character through justice, mercy, honesty and worship from the heart. The importance of repentance is restored relationship with God, forgiveness and renewal of the community; refusing to repent brings judgment.
sla_notes_illustrations: A businessman who has cheated customers repents by confessing, stopping the practice, repaying those he cheated and then living honestly; this matches Isaiah's call to wash, cease evil and learn to do good.
sla_notes_daily_life: Repentance is practised when people apologise, make amends and change habits such as corruption, drunkenness or gossip, and a holy life shows in honest work and care for the poor.

sla_notes_intro: Amos was a prophet who defended the poor and condemned injustice in Israel. His book teaches that God demands justice in society.
sla_notes_details: Amos was a shepherd and dresser of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah, called to prophesy in the northern kingdom of Israel around 760 BC in the reign of Jeroboam II, a time of prosperity but great inequality. Social justice means fair treatment, fair sharing of resources and protection of the rights of all, especially the weak. Amos opens with oracles against the nations and then against Israel. He condemns those who sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals (2:6), trample the head of the poor, deny justice in the gate, use dishonest scales and sell the refuse of wheat (8:4-6), and live in luxury while ignoring ruin (6:1-6). The wealthy women of Samaria, called cows of Bashan, oppress the poor (4:1). Their worship is rejected: I hate your feasts, but let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream (5:21-24). Violations of community rights lead to judgment and exile.
sla_notes_illustrations: The use of false scales in the market that Amos condemned is like a trader who uses a tampered weighing machine; God sees such cheating and Amos says it will bring judgment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Amos speaks to modern issues such as land grabbing, exploitation of workers, corruption in courts and unfair pay, calling believers to campaign for justice.
sla_exercise: Where did Amos come from and what was his work?::He came from Tekoa in Judah and was a shepherd and dresser of sycamore figs.||Name two sins of Israel condemned by Amos.::Selling the poor for silver or sandals, using dishonest scales, or luxury at the expense of the poor.||What does Amos 5:24 say?::Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.||Define social justice.::Fair treatment and fair sharing of resources so that everyone's rights are protected.

sla_notes_intro: Hosea shows God's steadfast love for unfaithful Israel through the prophet's own marriage. It teaches compassion, mercy and forgiveness.
sla_notes_details: Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel from about 750 to 722 BC, until Samaria fell to Assyria. At God's command he married Gomer, who was unfaithful, and their marriage becomes a picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to God through idolatry and Baal worship. His children were named Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah (not pitied) and Lo-ammi (not my people), signs of judgment. Yet in chapter 3 Hosea buys back Gomer and loves her again, showing God's persistent love. God's compassion and mercy (Hebrew hesed, steadfast love) appear in 6:6, I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, and in chapter 11 where God, like a parent teaching Ephraim to walk, says, How can I give you up? The book ends with a call to return to the Lord and a promise that God will heal their faithlessness and love them freely (14:1-4). Forgiveness is important because it restores broken relationships and shows how believers should treat those who wrong them.
sla_notes_illustrations: When Hosea took back Gomer who had left him, he forgave in action; this illustrates a parent who welcomes back a wayward child and pays the cost of restoration.
sla_notes_daily_life: Forgiveness and mercy heal marriages, families and communities, for example when a spouse forgives repentant unfaithfulness or a community accepts back a person who has changed.
sla_exercise: Whom did Hosea marry?::Gomer, an unfaithful woman.||What did Hosea's marriage symbolise?::God's love for unfaithful Israel.||Explain the name Lo-ammi.::It means not my people, a sign of God's rejection because of Israel's sin.||What does Hosea 6:6 teach?::God desires steadfast love and knowledge of him more than sacrifices.

sla_notes_intro: Haggai and Zechariah prophesied to Jews who had returned from exile. They urged the people to take responsibility for rebuilding the temple and living faithfully.
sla_notes_details: After Cyrus allowed the exiles to return in 538 BC, work on the temple began under Zerubbabel but stopped because of opposition and the people's concern for their own houses. In 520 BC, in the second year of Darius, Haggai asked, Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in paneled houses while this house lies in ruins? He told them to consider their ways: they sowed much but harvested little because they neglected God's house (Haggai 1:4-11). Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest and the people obeyed, and the temple was finished in 516 BC (Ezra 6:15). Zechariah, who prophesied at the same time, encouraged leaders with visions and the message not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (4:6), called the people to return to the Lord (1:3) and taught justice, mercy and compassion (7:9-10). Responsibility means fulfilling duties given by God: leaders to guide, priests to lead worship, and the people to give and work.
sla_notes_illustrations: The people plastered their own houses while God's house lay in ruins; Haggai's rebuke and their response show that putting God's work first brings his blessing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Responsibility is seen when citizens complete community projects, parents provide for children, and church members support their place of worship and the needy.

sla_notes_intro: A project lets students investigate a problem related to Divinity and apply their knowledge in a real setting. In Form Five students design the project and begin to collect data.
sla_notes_details: A research project follows steps. First identify a relevant problem, for example the effect of corruption on communities in the light of the teaching of Amos, or the role of the church in promoting forgiveness. Then write a title, background, statement of the problem, objectives and research questions. Review relevant Bible passages, commentaries and other texts. Choose methods such as interviews with pastors, questionnaires to youth, observation of church activities and reading of biblical texts, and plan sampling and ethical rules such as consent and confidentiality. Draw up a work plan and budget, then begin collecting data and keep records. Progress is presented to the teacher and classmates for feedback. The report will be completed in Form Six.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group chooses the topic The role of religious leaders in promoting social justice in our ward, links it with the book of Amos, interviews five leaders using a questionnaire and records their answers.
sla_notes_daily_life: Project skills such as planning, research, communication and teamwork help in higher education, and the findings help churches and communities solve real problems.

sla_notes_intro: The word gospel means good news. The Gospel according to Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and presents Jesus as the promised Messiah and King.
sla_notes_details: The word gospel comes from the Old English godspel, translating the Greek euangelion, meaning good news about Jesus Christ, his life, death and resurrection. There are four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, and the first three are called the Synoptic Gospels because they share a common view. Matthew was a tax collector called by Jesus to be an apostle (Matthew 9:9). The Gospel was probably written between AD 70 and 90 for Jewish Christians, using Mark and other sources. It begins with a genealogy tracing Jesus from Abraham through David, and it often says this was to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet, showing that Jesus fulfils the Old Testament. Matthew stresses the kingdom of heaven, Jesus as the new Moses who teaches with authority, and the church. His teaching is arranged in five discourses: the Sermon on the Mount (5-7), the mission discourse (10), the parables (13), the discourse on community life (18) and teaching on the end times (24-25).
sla_notes_illustrations: Matthew's genealogy begins Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and continues to David and Joseph, husband of Mary, proving to Jewish readers that Jesus is the Son of David and the son of Abraham.
sla_notes_daily_life: The good news in Matthew is shared today in preaching, Sunday schools, radio and personal witness, offering hope, forgiveness and a way of life based on the kingdom of God.

sla_notes_intro: Matthew describes Jesus' ministry from his birth to the resurrection. It shows Jesus teaching, healing and calling people into the kingdom of heaven.
sla_notes_details: Matthew records the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem, the visit of the Magi and the flight to Egypt (chapters 1-2). Jesus is baptised by John and tempted in the wilderness (3-4), then begins to preach repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand and calls his first disciples. The Sermon on the Mount (5-7) contains the Beatitudes, teaching on the law, prayer including the Lord's Prayer, and the Golden Rule. Chapters 8-9 present ten miracles of healing and power, including cleansing a leper, calming the storm and raising Jairus' daughter. Jesus sends out the Twelve (10), teaches in parables such as the sower and the mustard seed (13), feeds five thousand (14), and hears Peter confess that he is the Christ, the Son of the living God (16:16). He is transfigured (17), teaches on forgiveness and greatness (18), enters Jerusalem, cleanses the temple, is betrayed, crucified and raised on the third day (21-28). The Gospel ends with the Great Commission: go and make disciples of all nations (28:19-20).
sla_notes_illustrations: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus taught that the merciful are blessed and that his followers are salt of the earth and light of the world, giving a picture of the ethics of the kingdom.
sla_notes_daily_life: Jesus' ministry gives a model for church and social work: teaching the people, healing the sick, feeding the hungry and welcoming outcasts.
sla_exercise: Where did Peter make his confession that Jesus is the Christ?::At Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16:13-16).||Name one section of teaching in Matthew that includes the Beatitudes.::The Sermon on the Mount, chapters 5-7.||What is the Great Commission?::Jesus' command to go and make disciples of all nations, baptising and teaching them (Matthew 28:19-20).||Mention two miracles recorded in Matthew 8-9.::Healing a leper and calming the storm (also raising Jairus' daughter).

sla_notes_intro: Although the society of Jesus' time was dominated by men, Matthew mentions women at important points. They appear in the genealogy, in miracle stories and at the cross and the tomb.
sla_notes_details: Matthew's genealogy includes four unusual women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba (called the wife of Uriah), together with Mary the mother of Jesus, showing that God works through people of different backgrounds, including Gentiles. Mary, betrothed to Joseph, conceives by the Holy Spirit. Jesus heals Peter's mother-in-law (8:14-15) and the woman with a flow of blood who touches his garment (9:20-22). The Canaanite woman shows great faith and her daughter is healed (15:21-28). The mother of James and John asks for places of honour for her sons (20:20-21). A woman anoints Jesus at Bethany and he says her act will be told in memory of her (26:6-13). Pilate's wife warns him not to harm this righteous man (27:19). Many women watched the crucifixion from afar, and Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to the tomb, were first to hear that Jesus was risen and were told to tell the disciples (28:1-10).
sla_notes_illustrations: The Canaanite woman kept asking for help for her daughter, and Jesus said, Woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish, and the girl was healed at that moment.
sla_notes_daily_life: The stories affirm the dignity and contribution of women in the church and society, encourage their leadership and challenge cultural practices that exclude or belittle them.

sla_notes_intro: The Gospel according to John is the fourth Gospel and differs from the other three. It shows Jesus as the Word made flesh, the Son of God who gives eternal life.
sla_notes_details: Tradition holds that the author is John the son of Zebedee, the beloved disciple, and that it was written about AD 90-100, probably at Ephesus. John does not begin with a genealogy but with the prologue: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and the Word became flesh (1:1-14). The purpose is given in 20:31: these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name. John records seven signs, including changing water into wine at Cana, healing the official's son, feeding the five thousand, giving sight to the man born blind and raising Lazarus. He also records the seven I am sayings such as I am the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, and the way, the truth and the life. The Holy Spirit is promised as the Counsellor.
sla_notes_illustrations: When Jesus said I am the light of the world and healed the man born blind (John 8-9), the miracle was a sign pointing to his identity as the giver of spiritual sight.
sla_notes_daily_life: John's message of life, light and truth helps believers face doubt, encourages evangelism and supports the study of faith in the church and in school.
sla_exercise: What is the purpose of John's Gospel?::That readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (John 20:31).||How does John begin his Gospel?::With the prologue: In the beginning was the Word.||Give two of the I am sayings.::I am the bread of life; I am the light of the world; I am the good shepherd (any two).||Name a sign performed at Cana.::Changing water into wine.

sla_notes_intro: John portrays Jesus as one who loves people personally and sacrificially. His love is seen in his words and actions until his death.
sla_notes_details: John 3:16 states that God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. John records that Jesus loved Martha, her sister Mary and Lazarus (11:5), and he wept at Lazarus' tomb (11:35) before raising him. At the Last Supper, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (13:1) and washed his disciples' feet as an example of humble service (13:1-17). He gave a new commandment: love one another as I have loved you (13:34-35), and taught that greater love has no one than this, that a person lay down his life for his friends (15:13). At the cross he cared for his mother by entrusting her to the beloved disciple (19:26-27). After the resurrection he forgave and restored Peter, asking three times, Do you love me? and commissioning him to feed his sheep (21:15-17). He also showed love by forgiving the woman caught in adultery (8:1-11) and by speaking to the Samaritan woman.
sla_notes_illustrations: In washing the disciples' feet, the Master did the task of the lowest servant, teaching that love means humble service to others.
sla_notes_daily_life: Love in action today means serving the sick, forgiving those who wrong us, caring for elderly parents and giving up personal comfort for the good of others.
sla_exercise: Which verse says God so loved the world?::John 3:16.||What did Jesus do to show humble love at the Last Supper?::He washed the disciples' feet.||State the new commandment given by Jesus.::Love one another as I have loved you.||How did Jesus restore Peter?::By asking him three times, Do you love me? and telling him to feed his sheep.

sla_notes_intro: In John, God's love is meant to flow through believers to other people. Jesus teaches that his followers must love each other and the world as he loved them.
sla_notes_details: Jesus says that as the Father has loved me, so have I loved you; abide in my love (15:9) and commands his disciples to love one another, for by this all people will know they are his disciples (13:35). God's love reaches across barriers: Jesus talks with the Samaritan woman, a person despised by Jews (chapter 4), accepts the night visit of Nicodemus (chapter 3), and heals the sick and the man born blind. As the good shepherd he lays down his life for the sheep (10:11). In his prayer he asks that believers may be one so that the world may know that God sent him and loved them (17:20-23). He sends the disciples as the Father sent him (20:21). To show God's love to others, believers should feed the hungry, forgive, reconcile, welcome strangers, avoid tribalism and share the good news, as love is proved by deeds.
sla_notes_illustrations: A church that runs a feeding programme for street children and welcomes them without conditions shows God's love as Jesus did to the Samaritan woman by crossing social barriers.
sla_notes_daily_life: In society this love appears in charity, peace-making, volunteering and support for orphans, widows and the sick, regardless of tribe, religion or status.
sla_exercise: According to John 13:35 how will all people know that we are disciples of Jesus?::If we have love for one another.||Which person did Jesus meet at the well who was despised by Jews?::The Samaritan woman.||Why did Jesus pray that believers be one in John 17?::So that the world may know that God sent him and loved them.||Give two practical ways of showing God's love to others.::Feeding the hungry and forgiving or reconciling people (also caring for orphans and the sick).

sla_notes_intro: Romans is Paul's longest and most systematic letter, written to the Christians in Rome. Paul had several reasons for writing it.
sla_notes_details: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth about AD 56-57, at the end of his third missionary journey, while carrying the collection for the poor in Jerusalem. He had not founded the church in Rome, which had Jewish and Gentile members; Jews had been expelled by Claudius about AD 49 and had later returned, causing tensions. His reasons were: to introduce himself and his gospel before visiting Rome and to ask for support for a mission to Spain (15:22-29); to explain that the gospel is the power of God for salvation to all who believe, Jew and Greek (1:16-17), and that all have sinned and are justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law (3:21-26; 5:1); to unite Jews and Gentiles and show that God has not rejected Israel (chapters 9-11); to exhort believers to holy living (12-13); and to settle disputes between strong and weak believers over food and days (14-15). The letter ends with greetings to many named individuals in chapter 16.
sla_notes_illustrations: In chapter 14 the strong who ate all foods and the weak who ate only vegetables were told not to despise or judge each other; Paul used a practical dispute to show the unity of the church.
sla_notes_daily_life: The letter guides today's churches to handle divisions over tribe, denomination or customs with love, and it assures believers of salvation by faith rather than by achievement.
sla_exercise: From which city did Paul write Romans?::Corinth.||Which mission did Paul hope to start after visiting Rome?::A mission to Spain.||What is the central theme of Romans 1:16-17?::The gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, and the righteous live by faith.||Which two groups were in the church in Rome?::Jewish Christians and Gentile Christians.

sla_notes_intro: In Romans 13:1-7 Paul discusses the relationship between Christians and the governing authorities. It sets out duties for both rulers and citizens.
sla_notes_details: Paul writes that every person should be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God (13:1). The ruler is God's servant for your good and bears the sword to punish wrongdoers (13:4). Obligations of rulers therefore include promoting good, restraining evil, administering justice fairly and using power responsibly; the right of rulers is to receive respect, honour and taxes. Obligations of subjects include obeying laws, paying taxes and revenue, giving respect and honour, and obeying for the sake of conscience (13:5-7). The rights of subjects are protection, justice and order. Paul teaches that the state is under God, so it is not absolute; other passages like Acts 5:29 show that believers must obey God rather than human beings when the state commands evil. Paul wrote in the early years of Nero when Roman rule was relatively orderly, and some Christians in Rome may have refused taxes.
sla_notes_illustrations: A citizen who pays the correct tax and follows traffic rules fulfils Romans 13, while a ruler who uses tax money to build schools and hospitals fulfils his duty as God's servant for good.
sla_notes_daily_life: The teaching applies to modern life: citizens should vote, pay taxes and obey laws, and leaders must fight corruption, protect the poor and rule justly.
sla_exercise: According to Romans 13 who instituted the governing authorities?::God.||State two obligations of subjects in Romans 13.::Obey the authorities and pay taxes, revenue, respect and honour.||State two obligations of rulers according to Romans 13.::Reward the good, punish wrongdoers and rule justly as God's servants.||Give a biblical example when believers may refuse to obey rulers.::Acts 5:29: we must obey God rather than men.

sla_notes_intro: James is a short general epistle written to Jewish Christians scattered abroad. It gives practical advice on how to live the Christian faith.
sla_notes_details: The author calls himself James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and is usually identified with James the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15; Galatians 1:19). It is addressed to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion, that is, Jewish Christians outside Palestine, and it was probably written between AD 45 and 60, one of the earliest New Testament letters. It is called a general or catholic epistle because it is not addressed to one local church. The reasons for writing include: to encourage believers suffering trials and to teach patience (1:2-4, 5:7-11); to warn that faith without works is dead (2:14-26); to condemn favouritism towards the rich (2:1-13); to correct misuse of the tongue (3:1-12); to warn against worldliness, quarrels and boasting (4:1-17); to rebuke the oppression of workers by rich landowners (5:1-6); and to urge prayer for the sick and confession of sins (5:13-16). Its style resembles wisdom literature, with short commands and vivid images.
sla_notes_illustrations: James compares the tongue to a small rudder that steers a big ship and a spark that starts a forest fire, showing why his letter warns about careless speech.
sla_notes_daily_life: The letter guides Christians to practical living such as honest business, fair pay, patience in suffering and kind speech in homes and workplaces.
sla_exercise: Who is traditionally identified as the author of James?::James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church.||To whom was the letter addressed?::The twelve tribes in the Dispersion, meaning Jewish Christians scattered abroad.||Give two reasons why James wrote the letter.::To encourage believers in trials and to teach that faith must be shown by works (also to condemn favouritism and misuse of the tongue).||Why is James called a general epistle?::It was addressed to a wide group of Christians rather than to one local church.

sla_notes_intro: James shows how words and attitudes can build or destroy relationships. He gives guidance for good communication and cooperation in the community.
sla_notes_details: James advises that everyone should be quick to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger (1:19), because human anger does not produce God's righteousness. Chapter 3 teaches that the tongue is small but powerful and can bless God and curse people, so believers should control speech and avoid slander (4:11). He says the wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason and full of mercy, and those who make peace sow in peace and reap a harvest of righteousness (3:17-18). Quarrels come from selfish desires, so believers should submit to God, resist the devil and humble themselves (4:1-10). Believers should keep their word without swearing, let their yes be yes and no be no (5:12), confess sins to one another and pray for one another (5:16), be patient like the farmer waiting for rain (5:7), and care for the needy instead of merely wishing them well (2:15-16). Methods for maintaining good relations are listening, honest speech, prayer, humility, mediation and helping others.
sla_notes_illustrations: Two neighbours quarrel over a boundary; a church elder listens to both, prays with them and helps them agree, which applies James 3:17-18 on peaceable and merciful wisdom.
sla_notes_daily_life: Good communication prevents conflicts in families, schools and workplaces; cooperation is shown in group work, cooperative societies and community projects.
sla_exercise: What three things does James 1:19 tell believers to be?::Quick to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger.||What does James say about the tongue?::It is small but powerful and can bless or curse, so it must be controlled.||According to James what causes quarrels?::Selfish desires and passions that battle within people.||Name two ways of maintaining good relations in the epistle.::Confessing sins to one another and praying for one another, being patient, or keeping promises honestly.

sla_notes_intro: James insists that true faith produces good deeds. Believing without acting is empty and cannot save.
sla_notes_details: Faith is trust in God, and works are actions that show that trust. James 2:14-26 asks what good it is if someone says he has faith but has no works, and gives the example of wishing a hungry person well without giving food. He concludes that faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead. Abraham is shown as justified by works when he offered Isaac, and Rahab when she received the messengers and sent them out another way. The faith of a person is like a body: as the body without the spirit is dead, so is faith without works. Believers are told to be doers of the word and not hearers only (1:22-25), to keep themselves unstained by the world and to look after orphans and widows in their affliction (1:27), and to endure trials with joy because testing produces steadfastness (1:2-4). James does not contradict Paul: Paul teaches that people are justified by faith, and James teaches that such faith shows itself in deeds.
sla_notes_illustrations: A believer who prays for a neighbour with no food but does not share any of his own maize demonstrates the dead faith James describes; giving the maize demonstrates faith in action.
sla_notes_daily_life: Faith in action includes visiting the sick, paying fair wages, giving to the needy, being honest at work and volunteering in the community.

sla_notes_intro: Prejudice is judging people unfairly because of their wealth, status or background. James condemns this favouritism as sin.
sla_notes_details: In James 2:1-13 he describes two visitors to the assembly: a rich man in fine clothes and gold ring who is given a good seat, and a poor man in shabby clothes who is told to stand or sit on the floor. James says that this makes distinctions among believers and turns them into judges with evil thoughts. He points out that God chose the poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, while the rich often oppress and drag believers to court. Showing partiality breaks the royal law, You shall love your neighbour as yourself (2:8) and makes the person guilty of the whole law. Mercy will triumph over judgment (2:13). The evils of prejudice include division in the church and society, injustice, humiliation of the poor, hatred, discrimination based on tribe, class, gender or disability and loss of unity. It is overcome by treating all people equally, showing mercy, and remembering that all are created by God.
sla_notes_illustrations: If a church usher gives the best seats to the wealthy and leaves the poor at the door, that is the favouritism that James condemned.
sla_notes_daily_life: Today prejudice appears in tribalism, racism, unequal treatment in hospitals and schools and stigma against the poor or disabled; believers must resist it and promote equality.

sla_notes_intro: In Form Six students complete the project started in Form Five and submit a written report. They also present the findings to the teacher and class.
sla_notes_details: A project report normally has a title page, declaration, acknowledgements, abstract, table of contents, introduction, statement of the problem and objectives, literature and biblical review, methodology, presentation and analysis of findings, discussion, conclusion and recommendations, references and appendices such as questionnaires. Data collected are organised in tables and summaries, analysed by themes and percentages, and interpreted using biblical teaching. References should be listed in a consistent style, for example author, year, title and publisher. The language must be clear and free from copied material. Ethical rules such as consent, confidentiality and honesty must be followed. Students then present the report orally with visual aids and respond to questions.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group that studied forgiveness in their community reports that most interviewees, for example 18 out of 20 (90 percent), said forgiveness had restored a broken relationship, and they link this with Hosea and Matthew 18.
sla_notes_daily_life: Writing and presenting a report builds communication, analytical and teamwork skills for further study and for church and community leadership.
sla_exercise: List four sections of a project report.::Introduction, methodology, findings and analysis, conclusion (also abstract, references).||What is the purpose of the recommendations section?::To suggest actions to solve the problem studied.||Why should sources be referenced?::To acknowledge other people's work, avoid plagiarism and let readers verify information.||What ethical rule protects the identity of respondents?::Confidentiality.
